write.desc: Monotone functions on intervals and the continuity of inverse functions: completeness, through sup and inf arguments, shows that monotone functions have one-sided limits everywhere and only countably many jump discontinuities, and these same facts show that the inverse of a continuous strictly monotone function on an interval is continuous, which is why n-th roots are continuous.

points.name: Monotone functions
points.what: State the definitions of increasing, strictly increasing, decreasing and strictly decreasing functions on a set, give examples and non-examples, and see that strictly monotone functions are injective and that their inverses are strictly monotone in the same direction.
outside: order properties of the real numbers

points.name: One-sided limits of a monotone function
points.what: Prove that an increasing function on an interval has a left limit equal to the sup of f(x) for x < c and a right limit equal to the inf of f(x) for x > c at every interior point, with f(c-) <= f(c) <= f(c+), plus the matching one-sided statements at the endpoints and for decreasing functions.
outside: definition of one-sided limits of a function
supremum and infimum and the completeness axiom (approximation property of the sup)

points.name: Discontinuities of monotone functions are jumps
points.what: Show that a monotone function is continuous at c exactly when f(c-) = f(c+) = f(c), so its only possible discontinuities are jump discontinuities, and measure each jump by f(c+) - f(c-); removable and essential discontinuities cannot occur.
outside: continuity in terms of one-sided limits

points.name: A monotone function has at most countably many discontinuities
points.what: Prove that the open jump intervals (f(c-), f(c+)) of an increasing function are pairwise disjoint, choose a rational number in each, and conclude that the set of discontinuities injects into Q and is countable; see an increasing function with a jump at every rational, built from a series of jumps 2^(-n) over an enumeration of Q.
outside: countable sets and the countability of Q
density of the rationals in R

points.name: A monotone function whose image is an interval is continuous
points.what: Prove that if f is monotone on an interval and f(I) is an interval, then f is continuous, because a jump would leave a gap in the image that f cannot fill.
outside: intervals characterised by the intermediate property (if a < y < b with a, b in the set, then y is in the set)

points.name: A continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone
points.what: Prove, using the intermediate value theorem, that a continuous one-to-one function on an interval cannot change direction and so is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.

points.name: Continuity of the inverse function
points.what: Prove that if f is continuous and strictly monotone on an interval I, then f(I) is an interval and the inverse f^(-1): f(I) -> I is strictly monotone and continuous, by applying the previous result to f^(-1), whose image I is an interval.
outside: the continuous image of an interval is an interval

points.name: n-th roots and other inverse functions are continuous
points.what: Apply the inverse function theorem to x^n on [0, infinity) (and on all of R for odd n) to get existence, uniqueness and continuity of n-th roots, then rational powers x^(m/n), and informally log as the inverse of exp and arcsin as the inverse of sin on [-pi/2, pi/2].
outside: behaviour of the familiar functions exp and sin (rigorous definitions deferred)

points.name: Why the interval hypothesis matters
points.what: Work through a counterexample such as f(x) = x on [0,1] and f(x) = x - 1 on (2,3], a continuous strictly increasing bijection onto [0,2] whose inverse is discontinuous at 1, and locate exactly where the proof of continuity of the inverse uses that the domain is an interval.

where.title: Bartle and Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd edition)
Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd edition)
where.detail: Chapter 4, Functional Limits and Continuity, exercises on monotone functions
